title: What should a customer-service AI be allowed to do?
summary: A practical way to decide what a customer-service AI may read, recommend, draft and execute, action by action, with the identity, policy and enforcement checks each permission needs.
body_markdown:
Published October 3, 2026 · Updated October 16, 2026


If you want AI to resolve customer requests, answering questions is only part of the ambition. An agent may also need to look up an order, change a record or arrange a refund. Giving it that ability brings the prospect of completing service work that would otherwise return to your team.


It also means granting access to business systems, including sensitive ERP data and actions that affect customers' accounts or money. The scope of that authority matters as much as the agent's ability to understand a request. Access broad enough to be useful still needs limits that your business can enforce.


The decision is which work to entrust to the agent and where a person must remain in control. For a refund, that could mean explaining the policy, preparing a refund for approval or issuing it within agreed limits. Those are different grants of authority, even if all three are described as "handling refunds."


## Write one permission per action


For each action, record what the AI may do, which records it may access, the rule it must follow, what enforces the limit and who owns the decision.


- **Read:** retrieve information the verified customer is entitled to see.
- **Recommend:** propose a next step to a person who decides.
- **Draft:** prepare a message or change for a person to review and release.
- **Execute:** complete an approved action without per-case human review.


These modes have different prerequisites. A draft still needs permission to use the underlying information. If the customer cannot be verified or the AI cannot read the account, moving down from execute to draft does not solve the access problem.


## Check policy before technical capability


During a 2026 demo for a fashion retailer evaluating Typewise, the service team identified an action it could not use: changing a delivery address. Company policy prohibited it. The team suggested guiding the customer to make the change with the carrier instead.


That was a policy constraint raised in a demo, not a deployed Typewise workflow. It illustrates why an available action is not automatically an authorized one. Ask the business owner what the team may do today, including exceptions, before connecting a write operation.


A second team evaluating Typewise described its existing manual process for duplicate event registrations. When staff were confident both registrations belonged to the same person, they invalidated the later one, retained the original and resent the valid confirmation. When uncertain, they kept both. They were not merging customer histories, and this was not an AI result.


For your workflow, identify the cost of a wrong decision. A duplicate record left for review may be preferable to combining two people's information incorrectly.


## Put the limit where the action happens


An instruction such as "ask for approval above this amount" can guide what the AI proposes. It should not be the only control preventing a payment or account change.


Ask the integration owner to demonstrate the actual enforcement. For example, the refund endpoint might reject an amount above the approved limit, require a reviewer's approval, or deny writes to the AI's service account. These are possible designs to verify in your systems, not a promise that a particular connector already supports them.


Check customer authorization as well as login. Being signed in does not entitle someone to every account. The system serving the records must restrict which ones that customer can read or change.


If the integration cannot enforce the required boundary, keep the action behind an appropriate human process or exclude it from the pilot. Do not describe a prompt as an access control.


## Verify completion and preserve uncertainty


A message saying "I've issued the refund" is not proof. Require confirmation from the system that performed the action.


If a request times out, the outcome is unknown. Check the original transaction's status before retrying; a missing response does not establish failure. Tell the customer confirmation is pending, and hand the case to a person with the transaction details if necessary.


Test the ordinary sequence too: a customer looks up an order, then asks to return it. Verify the next step receives the authorized context and performs any additional checks it needs. Passing each isolated action does not prove the conversation works.


## Make permission changes deliberate


Name who can add an action, widen access or remove human review. Record the reason and evidence for each change. Recheck the actual connector permissions against that record after changes or upgrades.


Moving from employee-reviewed drafts to autonomous customer replies changes the scope. Confirm whether the original assessment covers it rather than assuming it does. The[procurement evidence guide](https://www.typewise.app/blog/customer-service-ai-procurement-evidence) explains what to prepare for that discussion.


Start with one real request and write its permission record with the service owner and integration engineer. Then test the allowed action, a denied action and the[handoff when the AI must stop](https://www.typewise.app/blog/ai-human-handoff-ownership) .
